name: inheritance-mappers
intent: Organise the database mappers of an object inheritance hierarchy into a matching structure - one discriminating mapper, a mapper hierarchy that mirrors the domain, or independent per-class mappers - so that superclasses and subclasses can be saved and loaded polymorphically without duplicated mapping code or a mapper shape that contradicts the chosen inheritance-to-table strategy.
problem: A polymorphic domain hierarchy has been mapped to relational tables, and now the mappers have to be shaped: either every mapper re-implements the inherited column list, or a row cannot be turned into the right subclass, or the mapper silently contradicts the table strategy it was written for (writing subclass columns into a single-table schema, or forgetting the superclass slice of a joined row).
context: Object-relational persistence of a polymorphic domain model, whatever produced the mappers: hand-written mapper classes, a metadata-driven ORM, or a combination. It applies once a table strategy (Single Table, Class Table, Concrete Table Inheritance) has been chosen for the hierarchy and mappers must support both abstract (superclass) and concrete (subclass) loading and saving, plus polymorphic finds that instantiate the correct concrete class.
benefits: One place per class describes that class's columns, so adding a subclass means adding a mapper, not editing its parent's mapping code.
Abstract mapping behaviour (identity field handling, find/insert/update/delete protocol, session registration) is written once in the base mapper and shared by every class.
Polymorphic reads work: a query against the base class returns fully-formed subclass instances because the mapper structure carries the discriminator-to-class decision.
Superclass and subclass can each be saved and loaded on their own, which keeps partial loading (base columns only) legitimate instead of accidental.
The mapper shape stays consistent with the table strategy, so the mapping question ('which table holds which column') is answered once, at the structural level.
Testability: mapping behaviour is isolated behind mapper roles, so load and save can be exercised per class rather than through the whole persistence stack.
tradeoffs: The mapper hierarchy mirrors the domain hierarchy, so domain refactors (move a field to the base class, split a subclass) ripple through every affected mapper.
One mapper per class multiplies code and column lists; in hierarchies with many thin subclasses the mapper count grows much faster than the business value.
Class Table Inheritance forces ordered collaboration: the superclass mapper must load/save first, and the join or the second query is where the performance and consistency cost lives.
Discriminator values, sti keys and polymorphic identities are schema contracts: renaming a class or changing a type code breaks existing rows, and the breakage only shows up at load time.
A base-class query returns partially populated objects; callers that do not know about the mapper shape (or the lazy loading it relies on) are surprised by empty subclass fields and extra queries.
Generated mappers can drift from the strategy: annotation-driven stacks apply a default strategy (single table) unless it is stated, so the mapper shape is chosen accidentally.
Debugging spans more components: a wrong object or a lost column may originate in the discriminator mapping, the superclass/subclass hand-off, or the session's identity map, not in the SQL.

participants.responsibility: Declares the mapping protocol for the hierarchy (find/load/save/insert/update/delete) and implements the behaviour common to all classes, so concrete mappers inherit its contract instead of re-deriving it.
Maps exactly the columns owned by one class, delegates inherited state to the superclass mapper (or reads the shared row itself) and never touches another class's table.
Resolves the mapper that owns a row or a domain object - by discriminator value, polymorphic identity or runtime type - so polymorphic finds return the correct concrete class.
The polymorphic objects being mapped (abstract base plus concrete subclasses); its shape is what the mapper structure mirrors, and its invariants are what loading and saving must preserve.
Carries the type code (type column, sti key, discriminator column) that tells the registry which subclass a row represents and that is persisted with every write.

The chosen inheritance-to-table layout (Single Table, Class Table, Concrete Table Inheritance); it selects the mapper shape - one discriminating mapper, chained per-class mappers, or independent mappers.

use_cases: A claims or payment hierarchy where the shared columns live in a base table and each subclass adds its own table: the subclass mapper joins the base table, calls the superclass mapper for the base slice and fills the subclass slice.
A shallow hierarchy with few subclass-specific columns stored in one table with a type code: a single mapper resolves the class from the discriminator and never consults a second table.
An event or message hierarchy whose subclasses are read independently: each concrete mapper is standalone, and the duplicated base columns are the accepted price of never joining.

ORM-driven stacks that must still make the same decision explicitly — JPA @Inheritance(strategy = ...), EF Core TPH/TPT/TPC, SQLAlchemy polymorphic_identity/polymorphic_on, MikroORM discriminatorMap or inheritance: 'tpt'.
Polymorphic finders: one query against the base type must hand back a mix of Payment, CreditCardPayment and BankTransferPayment instances from the same result set.
Adding a new subclass to a shipped hierarchy without editing the superclass mapper, by registering a new concrete mapper plus its discriminator value.

JPA/Hibernate legacy schema: mapping a database that already has a discriminator column (possibly named differently) using @DiscriminatorColumn with a custom columnDefinition or @DiscriminatorFormula.
EF Core TPH to TPT migration: an existing single-table hierarchy needs to be split into separate tables to add NOT NULL constraints on subclass columns or to reduce NULL column overhead.

SQLAlchemy polymorphic_abstract: an intermediate abstract class in a domain hierarchy (e.g., a Java/C# abstract base that is not an entity) needs to be excluded from the mapper hierarchy while still allowing concrete leaf classes to inherit from it.

Domain model with a read-heavy polymorphic query path and write-heavy individual subclass saves: SINGLE_TABLE optimises the reads but requires careful discipline on nullable columns; use it when base-class queries dominate the workload.

Hibernate ORM/JPA hierarchy using @Inheritance(strategy = JOINED) maps superclass and subclass tables through primary-key joins, while SINGLE_TABLE uses a discriminator for polymorphic reads; the mapper registry must mirror the declared strategy.

EF Core model with TPH, TPT, or TPC inheritance: TPH resolves rows with a discriminator, TPT joins base and derived tables through foreign keys, and TPC gives each concrete table its inherited columns, so mapper shape follows the chosen workload and schema constraints.

SQLAlchemy 2.1 Declarative hierarchy using polymorphic_on and polymorphic_identity resolves concrete classes from base queries; joined inheritance assembles table slices with joins, while concrete polymorphic loading needs a UNION-style selectable and more configuration.
avoid_when: The model has no inheritance: a plain Data Mapper per class is the same work without the hierarchy, and there is no strategy to be consistent with.
The whole object graph is stored opaque (Serialized LOB) or the store is a document database, so there is no row mapping and therefore no mapper shape decision.
The hierarchy is read-only and reporting-shaped: views or hand-written SQL projections returning flat rows are simpler than a mapper hierarchy.
A dominant framework already owns the decision and you never touch the mappers - rebuilding the structure on top of the ORM's generated mappers adds a second, competing mapping.
The hierarchy is an implementation detail of one table (a type code plus two boolean columns) and never surfaces as a base-class query; a branch in a single mapper is enough.
anti_patterns: One monster mapper: a single class with a type switch that loads and saves every class in the hierarchy, duplicating column lists and re-deciding the type on every call.
Mapper shape chosen by framework default: inheriting the ORM's implicit single-table strategy and then hand-writing per-class mappers that expect per-class tables.
Mapper hierarchy that drifts from the domain: a new subclass added to the model but never registered, so rows of that type load as the base class.
Column lists copy-pasted between mappers instead of delegating inherited state, so the base columns are maintained in N places.
Using single table inheritance for a wide hierarchy because the mapper is 'simpler', producing a table of mostly NULL columns and no NOT NULL guarantees.
Testing only round-trips of the concrete classes and never a polymorphic base-class find, which is exactly where the mapper structure fails.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: what a class stores (domain) is decided separately from how a row becomes that class (mapper).
Open/closed principle: a new subclass arrives as a new mapper plus a registry entry, not as edits to the base mapper.
Single responsibility per mapper: one mapper maps one class's slice of the database, and the superclass mapper is called rather than re-implemented.
Consistency between structure and storage: the mapper shape is derived from the table strategy instead of being chosen independently of it.
Polymorphism preserved end to end: the type code is data, so the class to instantiate is decided once, in the mapper structure, and not at every call site.
best_practices: Pick the inheritance-to-table strategy first and let it dictate the mapper shape; write that decision down next to the mappers.
Keep one mapper per class and delegate inherited state to the superclass mapper (super.load/super.save) rather than copying base columns.
Centralise the discriminator/type-code-to-class decision in one registry or factory so load and save agree on the mapping.
Test both directions per class — a load returns the right subclass, a save writes exactly the right tables — plus one polymorphic base-class find.
Treat discriminator values as a schema contract: never reuse or rename them casually, and map rows with unknown values explicitly instead of falling through to the base class.
Keep partial (base-class) objects honest: either expose only base behaviour on them or make the subclass slice lazy, and document which one callers get.
Do not duplicate column lists across mappers; move them into metadata or a single projection when the same columns appear in several mappers.

JPA/Hibernate: prefer INTEGER discriminator type over STRING for better index efficiency, especially in large hierarchies; index the discriminator column as it is filtered in most polymorphic JPQL queries (Vlad Mihalcea).

JPA/Hibernate: @MappedSuperclass does not support polymorphic queries or associations — use it only when sharing state without polymorphic persistence needs; if you need polymorphic queries, switch to SINGLE_TABLE or JOINED.

JPA/Hibernate: in SINGLE_TABLE inheritance, avoid NOT NULL constraints on subclass-only columns — all subclasses share the row and nullability is inherited; use CHECK constraints or application-level validation instead.

EF Core: TPH is the default and generally the best-performing strategy; TPT (table-per-type) generates separate JOINs per level and shows inferior performance in most cases; TPC (table-per-concrete) avoids the JOIN but duplicates base columns.
EF Core: use .HasDiscriminator() to configure discriminator column name, type, and values explicitly; relying on EF's implicit discriminator naming is fragile across migrations.

EF Core: when using TPT, be aware that composite foreign-key constraints and indexes cannot span both inherited and declared properties in different tables — this limits referential integrity options.
SQLAlchemy: configure polymorphic_identity on every class in the hierarchy (including the root) and polymorphic_on on the base mapper; without these the ORM cannot resolve rows to concrete types.
SQLAlchemy: in joined table inheritance, the subclass table's primary key must also be a foreign key to the base table; using a separate non-PK column for the FK is supported but rarely needed.
SQLAlchemy: for deep inheritance hierarchies, use polymorphic_abstract on intermediate abstract classes to prevent the ORM from expecting a discriminator value for non-persistent base types.
Always index the discriminator column in SINGLE_TABLE and JOINED strategies; without an index, polymorphic base-class queries with discriminator filters degrade linearly with row count.

pitfalls: Skipping the registry and instantiating the base class for every row quietly loses polymorphism — the bug surfaces as missing subclass fields, not as an error.
Letting the mapper shape drift from the table strategy: a per-class mapper hierarchy over a single table duplicates the same row read N times.
No ordering discipline in class-table saving: writing the subclass row before the base row violates the foreign key.
Discriminator column not indexed: in SINGLE_TABLE hierarchies, base-class polymorphic queries with discriminator filters cause full table scans at high row counts.
JPA/Hibernate: using @MappedSuperclass and then expecting polymorphic queries or associations — the persistence provider ignores the superclass as a queryable entity.
JPA/Hibernate: default STRING discriminator type wastes index space in large hierarchies; use INTEGER discriminator type with explicit @DiscriminatorValue per subclass.
JPA/Hibernate TABLE_PER_CLASS: polymorphic queries generate UNION across all subclass tables, which degrades badly as the hierarchy grows — prefer SINGLE_TABLE or JOINED for polymorphic workloads.
EF Core: switching inheritance strategy on an existing database migrates the schema; EF Core does not automatically copy data between old and new table structures, requiring manual migration scripts.
EF Core TPT: querying the base class generates one JOIN per hierarchy level; a 5-level deep hierarchy produces 5 JOINs per row — profile before using TPT in performance-sensitive paths.

EF Core: when querying a derived type, EF Core adds a discriminator filter; when querying the base type, the filter is omitted. If the database contains rows with unknown discriminator values, the base query will throw at materialisation time unless IsComplete(false) is set.
SQLAlchemy: forgetting polymorphic_identity on a subclass means that type is never instantiated polymorphically — rows are silently loaded as the base class.

SQLAlchemy: concrete table inheritance with polymorphic_load='selectin' or 'joined' requires careful configuration of with_polymorphic on the base mapper; misconfiguration causes the wrong table to be queried.

ORM default strategy trap: JPA providers and EF Core both choose SINGLE_TABLE/TPH implicitly when no @Inheritance annotation or mapping is provided; this silent default can contradict the intended schema design.

Partial-loading surprise: a base-class query returns partially populated subclass objects; callers unaware of the mapper's lazy-loading contract trigger N+1 extra queries when accessing subclass fields.

Wrong move: choose EF Core TPT solely for a normalized-looking schema -> deep polymorphic queries produce large join-heavy SQL and poor performance -> instead benchmark representative workloads and retain TPT only when external schema constraints justify it.
